headline: Medium-risk pair: shared API/MCP pathways create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; no direct evidence of stronger isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Chatwoot can ingest external messages and exposes API integrations, while MemMachine exposes an MCP server and user-facing agent connectivity. That creates a plausible bridge where Chatwoot content could be forwarded into MemMachine as trusted context. No direct shared-channel evidence is provided, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Chatwoot content is forwarded into MemMachine without provenance labels, prompt injection is possible.
IF the MCP server accepts untrusted text as instructions, attacker-controlled support messages can steer downstream behavior.
mitigations: Disable automatic forwarding from Chatwoot to MemMachine.
Add provenance tags to all Chatwoot-derived text before MCP ingestion.
Require a human review step for any instruction-like content.
Restrict MemMachine MCP methods to read-only memory operations.
requires-engineering: implement content-sanitization and instruction/data separation at the bridge.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, orders, and messages, while MemMachine stores long-term user facts and conversational context. If the pair shares a workspace or API bridge, sensitive support data can be copied into persistent memory. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so this remains medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Chatwoot transcripts are written into MemMachine memory, customer data may persist beyond the support workflow.
IF either agent logs full payloads to external services, leakage scope expands to stored context.
mitigations: Block customer-data fields from being sent to MemMachine.
Redact orders, contact details, and message bodies before transfer.
Set short retention on any shared memory entries.
Review logs for accidental payload capture.
requires-engineering: enforce field-level allowlists at the integration boundary.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Chatwoot has broad network egress and multiple API integrations; MemMachine has allowlisted egress plus MCP-based tool access. Both can act on shared external resources if orchestrated together, creating overlapping write or side-effect paths. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, so conflict risk is real but not proven high.
conditions: IF both agents are granted write access to the same external service, concurrent updates can race.
IF the orchestrator does not serialize tool calls, duplicate or conflicting actions can occur.
mitigations: Assign one agent as the sole writer for each external system.
Serialize writes through a single queue or operator.
Disable overlapping integrations not needed for the workflow.
Use idempotency keys on outbound actions.
requires-engineering: add distributed locking for shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Chatwoot produces support messages and reports; MemMachine is designed to retain conversational context and expose it through an agent interface. If MemMachine treats Chatwoot output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can propagate into later decisions. The profiles do not show direct action-taking like email sending, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF Chatwoot summaries are stored as facts in MemMachine, downstream answers may inherit errors.
IF MemMachine uses Chatwoot output without verification, incorrect support data can cascade.
mitigations: Mark Chatwoot-derived content as untrusted.
Require citation or source links before MemMachine reuses a fact.
Add a verification step for any customer-facing summary.
Limit MemMachine to retrieval, not autonomous action, for Chatwoot-fed data.
requires-engineering: implement confidence and provenance propagation.

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot handles customer data and interaction history, while MemMachine stores long-term user facts and conversational context. That combination can create retention and subject-rights mismatches if support records are copied into persistent memory. No residency or certification mismatch is documented, so the compliance concern is medium, not high.
conditions: IF customer support records are mirrored into long-term memory, retention obligations may diverge.
IF deletion requests are handled in Chatwoot but not propagated to MemMachine, subject-rights handling fails.
mitigations: Document which fields may be retained in MemMachine.
Mirror deletion requests from Chatwoot into MemMachine.
Set a retention timer for copied support data.
Restrict MemMachine to non-PII summaries.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows across both systems.
